top.content1: The OpenEmux manual: installing, importing games, cover art, views, playlists, favorites, cores, shaders and every settings page, with screenshots.
top.content3: How to install and use OpenEmux, section by section, with screenshots.
top.a30: The artwork items of a game
start.p1:
This manual walks through OpenEmux one part at a time, from installing it to the last
            switch in Settings. Each screenshot frames the part the text is talking about. Click any screenshot to see
            it full size.
what.p1: OpenEmux is a free and open-source emulation frontend. It keeps the games you already have organized by console, with cover art, and starts them with the controls and shaders already set. The emulation itself is done by RetroArch and its libretro cores; OpenEmux takes care of what is around it, so you do not have to learn RetroArch's menus before playing.
what.p2: OpenEmux does not come with games, ROMs or BIOS files. You add your own.
what.p3: Linux is OpenEmux's main platform. Windows is supported too, with a build that is still in beta.
window.alt1: The OpenEmux window showing a Super Nintendo library in the cartridge view
window.figcaption1: The main window, on the Super Nintendo page in the cartridge view.
window.p1: The sidebar lists the pages of your library, top to bottom:
window.li1: All: every game, grouped by console.
window.li2: Favorites: the games you starred. The row only appears once something is starred. See Favorites.
window.li3: Your playlists, if you made any. Here, Megaman. See Playlists.
window.li4: One row per console that has games, written as its short id and its name, like SFC - Super Nintendo (SNES).
window.p2: Console and playlist rows have a menu: right-click them, or hover and click the ⋮ button. Console rows can also be dragged to change their order.
window.alt3: The header bar, with the buttons on both sides framed
window.td2: Settings, Keyboard Shortcuts, Welcome, Report a Bug… and About OpenEmux.
window.td4: Rescans the console on screen, or every console on All. Same as F5.
window.td6: Opens the file picker to add games. See Importing games.
window.td8: Downloads missing artwork. See Syncing cover art.
window.td10: Opens Settings on the Input page. Only shown on a console's own page.
window.td14: Cover Grid, Cartridge Grid and Compact List. See Views.
window.td16: The layout menu: view, sorting, filter and thumbnail size for this page.
window.td17: Switches between the dark and the light theme.
window.td19: Filters the page on screen. See Search.
window.alt4: The bottom of the window: the sidebar buttons, the tips bar and the Log button
window.li5: Import ROMs and New playlist sit at the foot of the sidebar.
window.li6:
The tips bar shows a short tip that changes every few seconds. When you move around with the keyboard
              or a gamepad, it also shows which keys do what.
window.li7: Log opens the log panel. A red number on it counts errors. See When something goes wrong.
window.alt5: A cartridge card under the mouse, with the star, the menu button and the play button
window.p3: Pointing at a game shows three controls:
window.li8: the star at the top left marks it as a favorite;
window.li9: the ⋮ at the top right opens the game's menu;
window.li10: the play button in the middle starts it. A single click anywhere on the card does the same.
window.p4: Right-clicking a card also opens its menu.
window.h45: The main menu and the shortcuts
window.p5: Keyboard Shortcuts (Ctrl+?) lists the keys of the library. They are also in Shortcuts and hotkeys.
welcome.p1: The first time OpenEmux opens, a short tour walks through its main features: importing, layouts, cover art, colors and shaders, shortcuts, and keyboard and gamepad. You can pick the interface language on its first page. Untick Show on startup to stop it from opening by itself; it stays available from the main menu, under Welcome.
install.p1: Every release is on the Releases page. Pick the format that fits your system; all of them run the same app.
install-appimage.p1: One file that runs on most distributions without installing anything:
install-appimage.p2: If your system has no FUSE, start it with APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1 in front of the command.
install-deb.p1: Needs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or newer, or a Debian of the same age.
install-flatpak.p1: Sandboxed, and updated together with your other Flatpaks:
install-flatpak.p2: Updates then arrive with flatpak update. A single-file .flatpak bundle is on the Releases page too.
install-windows.p1:
Both Windows builds carry GTK 4, the Python runtime and RetroArch itself, so there is nothing else to
            install. They need Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.
install-windows.li1: Installer, OpenEmux-*-setup.exe: installs for your user only, so it does not ask for administrator rights. The builds are not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen warns about them; More info → Run anyway gets past it.
install-windows.li2: Portable, OpenEmux-*-windows-x86_64.zip: unzip it anywhere and run OpenEmux.exe from the OpenEmux\ folder inside. Useful on a USB stick or a machine where you cannot install software.
install-windows.p2: The Windows build is new. If something misbehaves, please open an issue.
install-verify.p1: Every release has a SHA256SUMS file. Put it next to what you downloaded and run:
install-verify.p2: OK means the file is exactly what was published. Anything else means it is damaged or was changed; do not run it. On Windows, PowerShell prints the hash and you compare it with the matching line in SHA256SUMS:
install-first.p1: The first time it runs, OpenEmux shows a Preparing first-time setup window while it creates its configuration, makes the ROMs, BIOS and covers folders, prepares input profiles and playlists, and downloads the libretro cores your consoles need. That usually takes about ten seconds; the rest of the cores keep downloading in the background while you use the app, and a banner under the header shows their progress.
install-first.p2: Your settings live in ~/.openemux/, and your games in ~/games/roms/, one folder per console.
install-source.p1: See the build instructions for the details.
import.p1:
OpenEmux plays the ROM files you already have. Importing copies them (or links them) into the ROMs
            folder, one sub-folder per console, and adds them to the library.
import-picker.alt1: The two Import ROMs buttons, framed: one at the foot of the sidebar and one in the header
import-picker.p1: Click Import ROMs at the foot of the sidebar or the ⤓ button in the header, or press Ctrl+O. A file picker opens; you can select several files at once.
import-picker.alt2: The Import ROMs file picker, with the ROMs and archives filter framed
import-picker.p2: The ROMs and archives filter shows only the files OpenEmux knows how to import, including .zip archives. When the import is done, a message says how many games came in and how many files were skipped, and OpenEmux looks for artwork for the new games.
import-picker.div1: Zip files. A zip is placed by the files inside it. If the console's core cannot read games from a zip, OpenEmux unpacks it for you and says so.
import-drop.p1: You can also drop files, or whole folders, anywhere on the window. While you drag, a banner says Drop the files here to import them. Folders are searched all the way down.
import-console.p1: OpenEmux decides the console from the file extension (.sfc is a Super Nintendo game, .gba a Game Boy Advance one, and so on). Two dialogs can come up along the way:
import-console.li1: When you import from All, Favorites or an empty library, it asks Which console? first, with Detect automatically selected. Leave it on that unless you want to force every file onto one console.
import-console.li2: When an extension is shared by several consoles, like .bin or .iso, it asks once per extension, with one button per possible console. The most likely one comes first.
import-folder.alt1: Settings, Library page, the ROMs Folder group
import-folder.li1: Path is where the library lives. Choose… points it at another folder; the folder icon opens it in your file manager.
import-folder.li2: How ROMs are imported chooses between Copy the file (the default: the original stays where it was and the library gets its own copy) and Link to the original (no copy; the library points to where the file already is, so moving or deleting the original breaks the game).
import-folder.p2: You can also put files into the console folders yourself, for example ~/games/roms/SFC/, and rescan.
import-rescan.alt1: The Reload visible page button, framed
import-rescan.p1: The library is scanned every time OpenEmux starts. To pick up changes made outside the app, use ⟳ in the header (F5), Rescan this console in a console's menu, or Scan ROMs in Settings → Library, which lets you pick one console or all of them.
covers.p1: OpenEmux downloads two kinds of artwork: covers (the box art) and labels (the art on the cartridge sticker, used by the cartridge view). It only fetches what is missing; art you already have is left alone.
covers-sync.alt1: The Sync covers button in the header, framed
covers-sync.p1: Click 🖼 Sync covers in the header, or press Ctrl+Shift+S. On a console's page it syncs that console; anywhere else it syncs the whole library. A banner under the header shows the progress, with a Cancel button, and covers appear as they arrive.
covers-sync.p2: The same action is in a console's menu (Sync covers), in the bar that appears when several games are selected, and in Settings → Library → Maintenance, where you choose the console first.
covers-providers.alt1: Settings, Library page, the Artwork Providers group
covers-providers.p1:
Three sources are tried in order, top first; the ones below are fallbacks. Each row has arrows to move it
            up or down and a switch to turn it off.
covers-providers.li1: libretro thumbnails: box art from the community collection. No account needed.
covers-providers.li2: ScreenScraper: box art and cartridge labels, matched by the ROM's hash, so it finds games even when the file name is unusual.
covers-providers.li3: OpenEmux mirror: box art from the project's own set.
covers-screenscraper.alt1: Settings, Library page, the ScreenScraper Account group
covers-screenscraper.p1: ScreenScraper works without an account: OpenEmux ships with developer credentials and a shared quota. A free ScreenScraper account of your own gets its own daily quota, which is faster and more reliable for large libraries. Fill in ScreenScraper username and ScreenScraper password. Advanced holds a developer ID and password, which you only need if you have your own developer account.
artwork-missing.alt1: A Mega Drive page where three cartridges have blank labels, framed
artwork-missing.p1: When no label was found, the cartridge shows a blank sticker; when no cover was found, the cover view shows a Search artwork… button on the empty card. To list only those games, turn on Only without artwork in the layout menu.
artwork-menu.h31: The artwork items of a game
artwork-menu.alt1: A game's menu with Sync label and Label image framed
artwork-menu.p1: Right-click a game, or click its ⋮. The artwork items act on the label in the cartridge view and on the cover everywhere else, and their names change to match:
artwork-menu.li1: Sync label… / Sync cover… fetches this game's art right away. Unlike the library sync, it replaces the art the game already has.
artwork-menu.li2: Label image ▸ / Cover image ▸ holds the other three.
artwork-menu.li3: Manage label… opens the artwork manager, below.
artwork-menu.li4: Choose cartridge label image uses an image file from your computer as is.
artwork-menu.li5: Remove cartridge label image deletes the art the game has now. It only appears when there is something to remove.
artwork-manager.p1: The manager opens from Manage cover… / Manage label…, or from the Search artwork… button on an empty card. It has three tabs.
artwork-manager.alt1: The artwork manager on the Cover tab, with box art results
artwork-manager.alt2: The artwork manager on the Label tab, with label results
artwork-manager.li1: Name is the title used for the search. Edit it if the file name is not the game's real name.
artwork-manager.li2: Hash is the file's fingerprint, worked out for you.
artwork-manager.li3: Search by name and Search by hash query the providers. A hash search is exact; a name search is more forgiving.
artwork-manager.li4: Suggestions (Cover tab) proposes close titles from the game-name database, ranked by how similar they are, when the name does not match anything as written.
artwork-manager.p2: Click a result to pick it; it gets a check mark. Save applies it and keeps the window open; Done applies it and closes; Cancel closes without changing anything. The Label tab only exists for consoles with a cartridge view.
artwork-manager.alt3: The Import tab of the artwork manager, with its editing tools
artwork-manager.p3: Drop an image onto the tab, or click Add… to pick one. Then you can Crop it, flip it, rotate it, or Reset your edits, and choose under Save as whether it becomes the Cover or the Label.
artwork-color.p1: In the cartridge view, Cartridge color ▸ paints the shell of one game's cartridge: Default, or Black, White, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Teal, Blue, Purple, Pink, Gold or Clear. Handy for the games that came on a colored cartridge, like the red Pokémon FireRed.
views-modes.p1: The three linked buttons in the header switch how the page shows its games.
views-modes.alt1: Cover Grid view, with its button framed
views-modes.figcaption1: Cover Grid: the full box art of each game.
views-modes.alt2: Cartridge Grid view, with its button framed
views-modes.figcaption2: Cartridge Grid (the default): each game drawn on its console's cartridge, with its label on the sticker. NES, SNES, N64, Game Boy, Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, DS, Mega Drive and Master System have cartridges; other consoles show their covers.
views-modes.alt3: Compact List view, with its button framed
views-modes.figcaption3: Compact List: one row per game, with a checkbox for selecting, a small thumbnail, the title and the console.
views-layout.p1: The ▦ View mode button opens the layout of the page on screen:
views-layout.li1: Use the global layout: when ticked, this page follows the layout shared by every page that has not got its own. Change anything below while it is unticked and the page keeps its own layout.
views-layout.li3: Sort by: Name (A-Z), Name (Z-A), Recently played, Recently added, File size and, on pages that mix consoles, Platform.
views-layout.li4: Only without artwork: shows only the games still missing art. It lasts until you close OpenEmux.
views-layout.li5: The − / + buttons set the thumbnail size, from 50% to 200%. Ctrl++, Ctrl+− and Ctrl+0 do the same.
views-layout.alt3: A console's menu with the Layout submenu, framed
views-layout.p2: A console's menu in the sidebar has the same choice under Layout ▸, so each console can keep its own view. Playlists have it too.
views-pages.alt1: The All page, grouped by console, with the All row framed
views-pages.p1: All, Favorites and playlists mix consoles, so they are grouped: each group has a header with the console's icon, name and number of games. Groups follow the console order you set in the sidebar or in Settings → Library.
views-search.alt1: The search bar with mario typed, filtering the All page
views-search.p1: Click 🔍, press Ctrl+F, or just start typing. The search filters the page on screen, so search from All to look through the whole library. Esc closes it.
views-select.alt1: The selection bar, framed, with two games selected
views-select.p1: A single click starts a game, so selecting works with modifiers: Ctrl-click adds a game, Shift-click adds a range, dragging on empty space draws a selection box, and Ctrl+A selects the whole page. In the list view, use the checkboxes. A bar appears at the bottom with Select all, Sync covers and Delete; the game menu's Add to playlist then acts on the whole selection. Click empty space, or ×, to clear it.
playlists.p1:
A playlist is a list of games you put together yourself, from any console: a series, the games you play
            with friends, the ones you are going through now. Adding a game to a playlist does not copy or move it.
playlists-create.p1: Click New playlist at the foot of the sidebar (or right-click empty space in the sidebar), type a name and click Create. The playlist appears in the sidebar, between Favorites and the consoles.
playlists-add.alt1: The Add to playlist submenu, framed
playlists-add.p1: In a game's menu, Add to playlist ▸ lists your playlists. A check mark means the game is already in it, and clicking a checked playlist takes the game out. New playlist at the bottom creates one with this game already in it. With several games selected, they all go in at once.
playlists-add.alt2: The Megaman playlist, with games from Super Nintendo and PlayStation
playlists-add.p2: Inside a playlist, games are grouped by console, and the game menu has an extra item, Remove from this playlist.
playlists-manage.alt1: A playlist's menu in the sidebar, framed
playlists-manage.p1: Right-click the playlist in the sidebar, or click its ⋮: Rename playlist…, Layout ▸ and Delete playlist. Deleting a playlist never deletes its games.
favorites.alt1: A game's menu with Remove from favorites framed
favorites.p1: To star a game, click the star on its card, choose Add to favorites in its menu, or press Ctrl+D (Ⓨ on a gamepad). The same gestures take the star away.
favorites.p2: A starred game keeps its star badge on every page.
favorites.alt2: The Favorites page grouped by console, with its row framed
favorites.p3: The Favorites page gathers them, grouped by console. Its row shows up in the sidebar once you have starred a game, and OpenEmux opens on it when there is nothing else to come back to.
cores.p1: A core is the emulator RetroArch runs for a console: Super Nintendo has Snes9x, bsnes, Mesen-S and others. Each console starts on a sensible default, shown as Automatic (…). A shader changes how the picture is drawn: a CRT shader brings back the scanlines and curvature of an old TV, and Disabled shows the raw pixels.
cores.p2: Both can be set for a whole console and, on top of that, for a single game.
cores-game.li1: Core ▸ lists every installed core for the console. The first item, Automatic (…), follows the console's setting. If the core you pick needs BIOS files you do not have, OpenEmux tells you which ones.
cores-game.li2: Shader ▸ starts with Use console setting (…), then Disabled, Dot, Geom CRT, NewPixie CRT, zfast CRT, CRT Royale and Sharp Bilinear Simple. Turn on Show all shaders in Settings → Video to list every shader RetroArch has.
cores-console.alt1: A console's menu in the sidebar, framed
cores-console.p1: Right-click a console in the sidebar. Default core ▸ and Default shader ▸ set what every game of that console uses unless the game has its own choice. They are the same settings as Settings → Cores and Settings → Video → Shaders per Console. Out of the box, handhelds (Game Boy, Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, DS) use Dot and everything else Geom CRT.
cores-menus.td1: Add to favorites / Remove from favorites
cores-menus.td4: Downloads this game's art again, replacing the current one.
cores-menus.td6: Manage…, choose an image file, or remove the current art.
cores-menus.td8:
Starts the game from one of its ten save-state slots, each with its date. Empty slots are greyed
                  out.
cores-menus.td10: The core for this game only.
cores-menus.td12: The shader for this game only.
cores-menus.td14: The shell color in the cartridge view.
cores-menus.td16: Puts the game in a playlist, or takes it out.
cores-menus.td20: Opens the folder with the ROM file selected.
cores-menus.td22: Renames the game and its file, keeping the extension. <kbd>F2</kbd>.
cores-menus.td24: After asking, moves the file to the trash. <kbd>Delete</kbd>.
cores-menus.td28: Opens the import picker. The extension still decides the console.
cores-menus.td30: Downloads missing art for this console.
cores-menus.td32: Use global, or a view of its own.
cores-menus.td34: The core for the whole console.
cores-menus.td36: The shader for the whole console.
cores-menus.td38: Opens Settings → Input with this console selected.
cores-menus.td40: Opens the console's folder in the file manager.
cores-menus.td42:
Changes the console's place in the sidebar. <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>↑</kbd> / <kbd>↓</kbd>, or
                  drag the row.
settings.alt1: The Settings window open on the Library page, with the Settings button and the page tabs framed
settings.p1: Open Settings with the 🛠 button in the header, from the main menu, or with Ctrl+,. The pages are along the bottom: Library, BIOS, Input, Video, Cores and System. The 🔍 at the top left searches every page. Changes take effect right away; there is nothing to save, except in the controls editor.
settings-library.p1: Where the library lives and whether imports copy or link the files. See The ROMs folder.
settings-library.li1: Scan ROMs rebuilds the game lists from the folders. A dialog asks for the scope: all consoles, or one.
settings-library.li2: Sync Covers downloads missing art in the background, for all consoles or one.
settings-library.p2: The order of the consoles in the sidebar and in the groups of All, Favorites and playlists. Use the arrows, or drag consoles in the sidebar. Restore default order undoes it. A console you ordered keeps its place even while it has no games.
settings-library.p3: See Where artwork comes from and ScreenScraper account.
settings-bios.alt1: The BIOS page with two consoles opened, framed
settings-bios.p1: Some consoles need the firmware of the original machine, the BIOS, to run games. OpenEmux does not ship any; you copy your own into <ROMs folder>/<CONSOLE>/bios, for example ~/games/roms/PS/bios/.
settings-bios.li1: Each console that uses BIOS files has a row showing how many it has out of how many it knows, like 0/1. The folder button opens that console's BIOS folder.
settings-bios.li2: Open a row to see each file, marked Required BIOS or Optional BIOS, with ⚠ while it is missing and ✓ once it is there. A line with one of: is satisfied by any of the files listed; PlayStation, for example, accepts several regional BIOS files.
settings-bios.li3: ⟳ at the top re-checks after you copy files in.
settings-input.p1:
This page edits the controls of one console at a time. A game started afterwards uses them; if that
            console's game is running when you save, it restarts with your progress kept.
settings-input.li1: Console: which console you are editing. It starts on the console on screen.
settings-input.li2: Input device: Keyboard, or Gamepad Port 1 to 4. The keyboard and player 1's controller work at the same time. For ports 2 to 4, an Enable this port switch sends that player's mapping to RetroArch.
settings-input.li3: Controller type: what the emulated console is told is plugged in. For example, a PlayStation can get a DualShock (needed by games with analog control), a Mega Drive a 6-button pad (for Street Fighter II), a Super Nintendo a mouse or a multitap. Only shown for consoles that have options.
settings-input.li4: Analog stick as D-pad: lets the stick move the D-pad without remapping anything. The (forced) options apply it even when the core would not.
settings-input.li5: D-pad also moves the analog stick: the other way round, for 3D consoles such as the N64 or the PlayStation.
settings-input.li6: Analog deadzone: how far the stick has to move before it counts. Raise it if a stick that is not being touched makes the character drift.
settings-input.li7: Analog sensitivity: multiplies stick movement. 1.0 is normal.
settings-input.li8: Axis threshold: how far a stick or trigger must go to count as a button press.
settings-input.li10: Input latency: when input is read during a frame. Early is the most responsive and the least forgiving on a slow machine; Late is the default.
settings-input.li11: Game focus: grabs the keyboard while a game runs, so RetroArch's hotkeys do not steal keys a computer game needs. Off, when the menu closes, or when a game starts.
settings-input.li12: Use the game's own button names: shows each button's in-game action in the RetroArch menu, when the core provides it.
settings-input.p3: Auto-fire for games that want a button mashed. Bind the Turbo (modifier) key in Game Controls below.
settings-input.li13: Turbo period: frames per fire cycle. Lower is faster.
settings-input.li14: Turbo duty cycle: frames the button stays pressed in each cycle.
settings-input.li15: Turbo mode: Classic fires any button held together with the modifier; the two Single button modes fire one chosen button, toggled or held.
settings-input.p4: One row per button of the selected console. Click a binding and press the key or button you want; it shows Press key... while waiting, and Esc clears it. If that key was used elsewhere, OpenEmux frees it there and tells you.
settings-input.li16: Map all walks through every button in turn.
settings-input.li17: Reset defaults brings back the default mapping of this console.
settings-input.li18: Save keeps your changes. Remember it; this is the one place in Settings that needs saving.
settings-input.p5: Keys for RetroArch itself rather than for the game: menu, save and load state, save slots, volume, mute, fast-forward, fullscreen, restart, rewind, pause, slow motion, screenshot, game focus and disk swapping. Enable hotkey is a button you hold to make the others work; on the keyboard it is empty by default, so the hotkeys work on their own. The defaults are in While playing.
settings-video.li1: View mode and Sort games by: the global layout. See The layout menu.
settings-video.li2: Show all shaders: lists every shader RetroArch has in the shader menus, instead of the short list.
settings-video.li3: Restore defaults: puts every console back on its default shader.
settings-video.p1: One row per console with its default shader. Same setting as Default shader in the console's menu.
settings-cores.alt2: The Super Nintendo core list open, framed
settings-cores.p1: One row per console. The subtitle says which core Automatic uses; open the list to choose another installed core. Same setting as Default core in the console's menu. A console with no core yet shows No core installed for this system until the background download gets to it.
settings-cores.p2:
Extra options that some cores understand, listed only for the consoles whose current core has them. For the
            PSP and PlayStation that means the internal resolution (render 3D games above their native resolution for a
            sharper picture, at a cost in speed), the graphics API and texture filtering.
settings-system.p1:
The interface language: English, Deutsch, 日本語, Français, 简体中文, Português (Brasil), Español or
            தமிழ். Settings reopens in the new language.
settings-system.li1: Theme: System (follows your desktop), Light or Dark.
settings-system.li2: Show tips: the rotating tip at the bottom of the window.
settings-system.li3: Control the interface with a gamepad: move around the library with a controller. Ⓐ confirms, Ⓑ goes back.
settings-system.p2: Whether the welcome tour opens at startup, and a button to open it now.
settings-system.p3: Show the log panel keeps the log open under the library; Report a bug copies the log and your system details and opens a report on GitHub. See When something goes wrong.
settings-system.p4: Export saves packs every save state and battery save (the in-game saves of cartridges) into one .zip. Import saves restores such a file, for example on a new computer; saves you already have are left alone.
settings-system.p5: Sign in with your RetroAchievements account to unlock achievements while you play. Your password is exchanged for a token once and is not stored. Once signed in, you can turn tracking on and choose Hardcore mode, which disables save states, rewind and fast-forward.
settings-system.p6: Shows whether the first-launch setup finished. If a step failed, for example because you were offline, Finish initial setup retries it in the background.
keys-library.td16: Switch between the sidebar and the games
keys-library.td18: From the console list into the games, and back
keys-library.td34: Extend the selection, toggle the focused game
keys-library.td36: Move the console up or down
keys-library.td38: Clear the selection, then go back to the sidebar
keys-game.p1: The default keyboard keys. Change them in Settings → Input → System Hotkeys.
keys-game.p2:
Default game keys: arrows for the D-pad, <kbd>Z</kbd> A, <kbd>X</kbd> B, <kbd>S</kbd> X, <kbd>C</kbd> Y,
            <kbd>D</kbd> / <kbd>A</kbd> L1 / R1, <kbd>E</kbd> / <kbd>Q</kbd> L2 / R2, <kbd>Enter</kbd> Start,
            <kbd>Space</kbd> Select, and <kbd>I</kbd> <kbd>J</kbd> <kbd>K</kbd> <kbd>L</kbd> for the analog stick.
keys-game.p3:
Games open in a window with a control bar at the bottom: close, menu, pause, reset, slow motion,
            fast-forward, turbo, save and load state, volume, fullscreen, and a button to hide the bar.
keys-gamepad.p1: In a game, Select is the hotkey button: Select+Start opens the RetroArch menu, Select+X saves a state, Select+Y loads it, Select+L1 toggles fullscreen and Select+R1 fast-forwards.
keys-gamepad.p2: In the library, with Control the interface with a gamepad on: Ⓐ plays, Ⓑ goes back, Ⓧ opens the game's menu, Ⓨ toggles favorite, L1 / R1 change console, and holding Ⓐ starts selecting games. The tips bar shows the buttons as you go.
help.alt1: The log panel open at the bottom of the window
help.p1: Click Log at the bottom right. The panel shows what OpenEmux is doing as it happens: scans, downloads, the exact command each game was started with, and why a game closed straight away. Copy Log + System Info puts it on the clipboard, and Report a Bug… walks you through opening a report on GitHub with it pasted in.
help.li1: A game closes as soon as it opens. The message usually says why. Check BIOS for consoles that need one, and try another core from the game's Core ▸ menu.
help.li2: A game has no art. Try Sync label… / Sync cover…, or search by another name in the artwork manager.
help.li3: The controller does nothing. Check it in Settings → Input with Input device on its port. On Linux, your user may need to be in the input group.
help.p3: Questions and ideas are welcome on r/OpenEmux, and bugs on GitHub.
